# Mixture of experts

Four sub-networks and a **gate** that decides how much each one gets to say. This is the
shape every frontier model is built from now, and it is small enough here to see all of at
once: 48 parameters, trains in seconds.

Each expert is a single `Linear` layer — a model far too simple to separate three spiral
arms on its own. The gate is also a single `Linear` layer, followed by a softmax, so its
four outputs are weights that sum to one. Each expert's answer is multiplied by its weight
and the four are added up.

**The claim this workflow actually tests:** does routing buy anything, or is it just a
roundabout way of spending parameters? Two controls are wired up beside it to answer that.
The answer turned out to be **not the one this note originally claimed** — see the table to
the right, and the seed column in particular.

Change the `seed` on the two Train nodes and run it again. The mixture will land in the same
place; the dense control may not.

## What routing buys — 8 seeds, two devices

| model | params | mean | spread (sd) |
|---|---|---|---|
| one `Linear`, alone | 9 | 0.371 | 0.022 |
| 4 linear experts + gate | 48 | **0.662** | **0.008** |
| dense MLP, 8 hidden | 51 | 0.603 | **0.082** |
| dense MLP, 12 hidden | 75 | 0.719 | 0.037 |
| 8 linear experts + gate | 96 | 0.715 | 0.019 |

**The reliable finding is the first two rows.** Chance is 0.333, so one linear model has
learned essentially nothing — three spiral arms cannot be cut apart by straight lines. Four
of those same helpless models plus a gate reach 0.662, because a mixture of linear models is
**piecewise** linear, and that is a different class of function entirely.

**The finding that did not survive is "routing beats dense".** An early 3-seed run had the
mixture ahead of the matched dense control by +0.075. With 8 seeds the gap is +0.059 on CPU
and **−0.021 on CUDA** — smaller than the combined spread of 0.065–0.082, and the sign flips
with the device. There is no difference in the means. Do not believe the first number you
get from three seeds.

**But look at the spread column, which is where the real difference is.** The 51-parameter
dense control ranges from **0.457 to 0.741** across seeds — it is bimodal, sometimes finding
a good solution and sometimes collapsing, and nothing but the initialisation decides which.
The mixture's spread is *ten times smaller*. At a matched budget, routing does not buy you a
better answer; it buys you **the same answer every time**.

## What routing does *not* do here

Look at the routing map. The gate is a `Linear` layer, so its boundaries are **straight
lines** — it can only cut the plane into four wedges. The spiral arms wrap through every
wedge, so every expert receives all three classes in roughly equal measure.

Measured purity — the largest class share inside an expert's own region — is **0.37 to
0.51**, against a floor of 0.33. Almost nothing. The gate has partitioned *space*, not
*meaning*.

Swap the dataset to `blobs` and re-run: three separated clumps, and the gate can isolate
them. But something worse shows up there — **two of the four experts received zero points**.
The gate sent everything to two of them and the other two never got a gradient again.

That is **expert collapse**, and it is the central practical problem with mixtures. Real
systems add a load-balancing term to the loss to prevent it. There is no such term here, so
you can watch it happen. The diagnostic is the **participation ratio**: 3.61 of 4 on
spirals, but as low as 2.0 on blobs.

## What this workflow *cannot* show

Be careful about the lesson. The reason frontier models use mixtures is **conditional
compute**: with hundreds of experts you run only the two or three the gate picks, so
capacity grows without the cost growing with it.

This gate is *soft*. Every expert runs on every point and then gets multiplied by a weight
that is often near zero. **There is no compute saving here at all** — the mixture costs
strictly more than the dense control it beats.

Getting the real thing needs top-k routing, which needs an op this pack does not have. What
is on the canvas is the *mechanism* — learned routing, visible specialisation, and
collapse — not the payoff.
